metadata.title: Using machine learning algorithms to predict students' general self-efficacy in PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the publicly available PISA 2018 microdata, merging Student Questionnaire and Principal Questionnaire responses at the student–principal level. The analytic sample was reduced by listwise deletion of cases with missing values on any of the five self-efficacy items (84,179 records removed), and then missing predictor values were imputed using median substitution. The manuscript does not report whether PISA complex survey weights (and any replicate weights) were applied in the ML training/evaluation pipeline, so weight usage cannot be confirmed. Because the models are XGBoost and Lasso implemented in Python/scikit-learn, the paper does not describe a weight-aware estimation approach; therefore, weighting is treated as not reported in the methods.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because the dependent variable is a transformed self-efficacy score derived from five Likert items using an IRT generalized partial credit model, rather than a PV-based cognitive achievement score. Missing data handling is partially reported: the authors explicitly used listwise deletion for missingness on the five self-efficacy items, and then median imputation for missing predictor values. The paper does not provide a single unified missing-data strategy for all variables beyond these two stages, but it does document the key steps for the outcome items and predictors.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 Student Questionnaire and Principal Questionnaire variables merged at the student–principal level. Eliminated all rows with missing data on any of the five self-efficacy items (listwise deletion), reducing the dataset to 527,825 records. For remaining cases, imputed missing predictor values by substituting median values. Included 256 predictors (including dummy variables) and one outcome variable (self-efficacy) derived from the five self-efficacy items via a polytomous IRT model.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (Student Questionnaire + Principal Questionnaire), general self-efficacy (5-item IRT score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (test set): RMSE=9.699, MAE=7.219, R²=0.467. Lasso (test set): RMSE=10.137, MAE=7.683, R²=0.417. Reduced model (top 14 predictors) R²=0.436; exclusion model (without top 14) R²=0.328.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (Student Questionnaire + Principal Questionnaire) the study leveraged mastery goal orientation, meaning of life, proud emotion, positive emotions, and learning aspiration to predict students’ self-efficacy (continuous IRT-transformed score), finding that XGBoost outperformed Lasso with higher test-set fit (R²=0.467 vs 0.417) and lower error (RMSE=9.699 vs 10.137). This indicates that affective and motivational variables—along with selected contextual factors—can support scalable ML-based monitoring of self-efficacy, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims and the paper does not report survey-weight usage.

data.outcome_summary: The study predicts students’ general self-efficacy using PISA 2018 Student Questionnaire and Principal Questionnaire data merged at the student–principal level across 79 countries/regions. Self-efficacy is operationalized as a continuous score derived from five Likert items via a polytomous IRT generalized partial credit model, then linearly transformed for interpretability. After listwise deletion of cases with missing self-efficacy items (reducing the sample to 527,825) and median imputation for missing predictors, the authors train two ML regressors—XGBoost and Lasso—using nested cross-validation (4 folds in both inner and outer loops) and evaluate with RMSE, MAE, and R². XGBoost achieves the best test performance (R²=0.467; RMSE=9.699; MAE=7.219), explaining about half the variability, while Lasso yields R²=0.417. The top predictors are dominated by motivational and affective constructs (e.g., mastery goal orientation, meaning of life, proud/positive emotions), and robustness checks show that a reduced set of top predictors retains substantial explanatory power (R²=0.436), whereas excluding them drops performance (R²=0.328). Limitations include the cross-sectional nature of PISA (no causal inference) and the absence of reported complex-survey weight application in the ML pipeline.
